title: He Read Love in My Glance and Warned Me
intro: A friend catches a look in al-Barudi’s eyes and sees the love he has tried to hide. The poet looks back to the day the women rode away, then follows a flash of lightning towards the place where their company might gather again. Muhammad Shafiq Ma'ruf, the diwan’s editor, connects the storm with the travellers through the pasture that springs up after rain and draws the tribes to camp there. The recitation ends among the curtained tents, one line before the poem’s call to make the most of youth.

translation: He read love in my glance and warned me,
a dear friend whose affection I cherished, who cared for me in turn.
1.sharh: Only in the second half do we learn who recognised that look. The same Arabic verb describes the care the speaker has taken of their friendship and the care his friend shows him now.

translation: I hid my secret from him. What gave it away
was a tear that breached the bounds of my silence.
2.sharh: The tear acts as an informer. He imagines his silence as land set aside and guarded against entry, yet his friend gains access to it without his saying a word.

translation: What excuse can I give to deny a burning grief
when the tears from my own eyes bear witness to it?
3.sharh: He imagines having to answer the charge of being in love. His own tears have already testified against him, so anything he might say in his defence comes too late.

translation: Friend, may you never see what love did
to your brother the day the litters went their separate ways.
4.sharh: He calls himself his friend’s brother and recalls the camel litters carrying the women away. Even to see what that parting did to him is an experience he would spare his friend.

translation: That day I lost my composure. I wasted away
with a longing that struck beneath my ribs and brought me down.
5.sharh: Shock costs him the composure that once helped him keep his secret. Grief reaches in under his ribs and strikes like an assailant who leaves him fallen.

translation: Peace to you from this heart of mine.
It followed love and went on without a rein.
6.sharh: He greets the friend he called on earlier, though his heart has already gone with the woman who rode away. He imagines it as a mount whose rider has lost the reins.

translation: It will hardly return now, caught as it is
by the glances of that beguiling young gazelle.
7.sharh: Her sidelong looks make him think of a young gazelle. His heart has slipped its rein only to be caught by her gaze.

translation: On the saddles ride Arab women
who can beguile even a wary man of sound judgement.
8.sharh: The scene widens from a single pair of eyes to the women riding out. Even a man who keeps his wits about him can have his judgement stolen by the sight.

translation: Until parting came so suddenly, I never knew
that lions could be the prey of gazelles.
9.sharh: The lions are the men, the gazelles the women. Only when the women leave does he realise which of the two has been at the other’s mercy.

translation: They left. How the tears poured down,
how my hand pressed against my pounding heart.
10.sharh: After the lions and gazelles, he shows what parting looks like in a single body. A hand presses against the chest as if it could steady the heart inside.

translation: How I longed for that flash of lightning
that held our gaze at Abraq al-Hannan.
11.sharh: The lightning gives longing a direction and holds the watchers’ eyes. A flash above a desert watering place raises the prospect of rain and of a camp gathering there.

translation: It races through the heart of the clouds,
a flame darting back and forth in a sky of smoke.
12.sharh: The flash races in and out of sight. For an instant the clouds look like smoke and the lightning like the flame that keeps showing through it.

translation: Look. Perhaps you can make out its caravan
and see where the winds will send its rain.
13.sharh: The lightning now has a caravan of its own, the clouds carrying the rain. The friend is asked to follow that caravan with his eyes and see where the rain will fall.

translation: That is where the tribes gather, where
tent fringes meet over branches of the ban tree.
14.sharh: Rain brings the scattered tribes to the same pasture. Behind the fringed curtains, the slender branches bring the women’s figures back into view at the moment he imagines finding their camp.

1.2.1.head: خِلّ
1.2.1.meaning: An intimate friend, someone whose affection can be trusted.

1.2.2.head: رَعى
1.2.2.meaning: To tend or look after. He has tended his friend’s affection, and his friend now looks after him.

2.1.3.head: سَريرَة
2.1.3.meaning: Something kept in the depths of the heart, an unspoken thought or feeling.

2.1.4.head: وَشى
2.1.4.meaning: To inform on someone or betray a confidence. Here the tears are the informers.

2.2.4-5.head: حِمى الكِتمان
2.2.4-5.meaning: “The preserve of my silence” pictures a secret as grazing land from which outsiders are kept.

3.1.4.head: لَوعَة
3.1.4.meaning: The burning pain of grief or longing.

3.2.3.head: عَبرَة
3.2.3.meaning: A tear. With a different first vowel, the same letters mean a lesson drawn from an event.

4.1.2.head: صاحِب
4.1.2.meaning: A friend or companion. In direct address sahib can lose its final consonant, as it does here.

4.1.3-4.meaning: “May you never see” is a wish that the friend be spared the sight.

4.2.4.head: ظَعينَة
4.2.4.meaning: A woman travelling in a covered camel litter, or the litter carrying her. The plural evokes the whole departing company.

5.1.3.head: حِلم
5.1.3.meaning: Composure, the ability to govern one’s feelings under strain.

5.1.5.head: شَفَّ
5.1.5.meaning: To wear someone thin or sap their strength through grief.

5.2.1.head: وَلَه
5.2.1.meaning: Grief or longing so intense that a person loses their bearings.

5.2.3.head: جانِحَة
5.2.3.meaning: One of the ribs towards the front of the chest. The plural also suggests the heart they enclose.

6.1.1.head: عَلى
6.1.1.meaning: “To you”, with a masculine ending in the recitation, as when he addressed his friend two lines earlier. Ma'ruf reads the greeting as addressed to the departing woman.

6.2.4-5.head: بِغَيرِ عِنان
6.2.4-5.meaning: “Without a rein.” A rein controls a mount, and the heart here runs free of its owner.

7.1.1.meaning: An expression meaning “far from likely”. It makes the heart’s return seem all but impossible.

7.2.1.head: لَحظَة
7.2.1.meaning: A glance, especially a sidelong look. The plural here means glances.

7.2.3.head: شادِن
7.2.3.meaning: A young gazelle strong enough to do without its mother. Its eyes and grace make it a figure for the beloved.

8.1.2.head: رِحالَة
8.1.2.meaning: A riding saddle. Raha'il is the plural of rihala, distinct from rahhala, a traveller.

8.2.2.head: لُبّ
8.2.2.meaning: The core or kernel of a thing, hence a person’s discerning mind.

9.1.5-6.head: بادِرَة النَّوى
9.1.5-6.meaning: “The onset of separation” is the moment the sudden departure takes him unawares.

9.2.3.head: فَريسَة
9.2.3.meaning: Prey seized by a beast of prey. The lions themselves occupy that place here.

10.1.4.head: مَسفوح
10.1.4.meaning: Poured out or shed freely, said of tears as well as other liquids.

10.2.3.head: حَشا
10.2.3.meaning: The organs within the ribs. Here it is the heart that pounds under the lover’s hand.

11.1.3.head: بارِق
11.1.3.meaning: A flash of lightning, also a cloud that gives off lightning. The gleam first catches their eyes.

11.1.4.head: شَخَصَ
11.1.4.meaning: Of a gaze, to become fixed, the eyes wide and unblinking.

11.2.3-4.head: أَبرَق الحَنّان
11.2.3-4.meaning: Abraq al-Hannan, a watering place of the Banu Fazara named in Yaqut’s geographical dictionary.

12.1.1.head: اِستَنَّ
12.1.1.meaning: To run freely back and forth, as a horse does. Here the movement is the lightning’s.

12.1.3.head: عُرض
12.1.3.meaning: The midst or interior of something. Here it is the mass of cloud through which the lightning races.

13.1.4.head: رِكاب
13.1.4.meaning: Riding camels, a collective noun. The moving banks of cloud form a caravan.

13.2.1-2.head: طَوع الرِّياح
13.2.1-2.meaning: “At the winds’ bidding”, moving wherever the winds drive it.

14.2.1.head: هُدب
14.2.1.meaning: The loose threads at the edge of a fabric, here the fringe of a hanging curtain.

14.2.2.head: خِدر
14.2.2.meaning: A curtained space set aside for a woman, also the curtain that encloses it. The reciter says khudud, “cheeks”. Both the diwan and its commentary give khudur, whose fabric has the fringe in this scene.

14.2.4-5.head: غُصون البان
14.2.4-5.meaning: “Branches of the ban tree.” The tree’s slender, supple branches are a conventional image for a woman’s figure.
